top_cited_works.title: Chemical, Thermal Stability, Seal Swell, and Emissions Studies of Alternative Jet Fuels
top_cited_works.abstract: This effort describes laboratory evaluations of six alternative (nonpetroleum) jet fuel candidates derived from coal, natural gas, camelina, and animal fat. Three of the fuels were produced via Fischer−Tropsch (FT) synthesis, while the other three were produced via extensive hydroprocessing. The thermal stability, elastomer swell capability, and combustion emissions of the alternative jet fuels were assessed. In addition, detailed chemical analysis was performed to provide insight into their performance and to infer potential behavior of these fuels if implemented. The fuels were supplied by Sasol, Shell, Rentech, UOP, and Syntroleum Corporation. Chemical analyses show that the alternative fuels were comprised of mostly paraffinic compounds at varying relative concentrations, contained negligible heteroatom species, and were mostly aromatic-free. The six paraffinic fuels demonstrated superior thermal oxidative stability compared to JP-8, and therefore, have increased resistance to carbon formation when heated and can be exposed to higher temperatures when used to cool aircraft systems. top_cited_works.title: Simulations of Flowing Mildly-Cracked Normal Alkanes Incorporating Proportional Product Distributions
top_cited_works.abstract: Hydrocarbon fuels have been used as a cooling media in aircraft jet engines for many years. However, advanced aircraft engines are reaching a practical heat transfer limit beyond which the sensible heat transfer provided by fuels is no longer adequate. One solution is to use an endothermic fuel that absorbs heat through chemical reactions. A two-dimensional computational model is developed to calculate the heat and mass transport associated with a flowing fuel using a unique global chemical kinetics model. Most past models do not account for changes in the chemical composition of a flowing fuel and also do not adequately predict flow properties in the supercritical regime. The two-dimensional computational model presented calculates the changing flow properties of a supercritical reacting fuel by use of experimentally derived proportional product distributions. The calculations are validated by measured experimental data obtained from a flow reactor in which n-decane and n-dodecane are mildly cracked. It is believed that these simulations will assist the fundamental understanding of high-temperature fuel flow experiments.

recent_works.title: Impact of clay treatment on aviation fuel thermal stability
recent_works.abstract: Rising concerns about jet fuel thermal stability have led to investigations into clay treatment as a potential solution. While traditionally used for removing surfactants and preventing fuel-water emulsions, clay treatment has shown promise in removing polar compounds that negatively impact thermal stability. The purpose of this project was to examine the effect of clay treatment (using drum quantity, clay treating equipment) on the chemical composition of thermally unstable (or marginal) fuels and to track the ability of clay to improve thermal stability. The adsorptive capacity of clay used in the treatment process was also evaluated. The impacts of surfactant on clay treatment efficiency for removal of heteroatomic species, and the understanding of the competitive interactions of heteroatomic species with the clay material were also of interest. Results confirmed that clay treatment can remove certain polar compounds responsible for thermal instability. Further investigation revealed that polar compounds exhibit varying degrees of attraction to clay, and the presence of certain compounds can displace others, potentially impacting thermal stability negatively. recent_works.title: Effect of Biodiesel on Jet Fuel Quality and Biodeterioration
recent_works.abstract: A prolonged and strong debate has been ongoing for about a decade on the merits of allowing increased levels of fatty acid methyl esters (FAME) from biodiesel in jet fuel. Currently, the jet fuel FAME limit stands at 50 ppm (50 mg/kg) from the pre-2015 limit of 5 ppm. Since then, multiple attempts have been made to further increase the FAME limit to 100 ppm and beyond. While clear economic factors lean to support raising the limit of FAME in jet fuel, known risk factors, such as the potential effect of FAME on jet fuel quality, properties, and degradability, serve as a strong counterbalance perspective due to safety. In this study, we provide strong, actionable scientific evidence for the fuel and aviation community to make informed decisions regarding allowing increased levels of FAME in jet fuel. Our methodical research approach supports that, besides the obvious physical issues with FAME in fuel, such as increased dissolved water content and phase separation, FAME concentrations above 100 ppm significantly increase the growth of microorganisms in jet fuel and the potential for biodeterioration.
